title: The rehatnamas
hook: codes of conduct linked to the Tenth Guru's time, written down by Sikhs after him

segments.voice: Yesterday, the poets of Anandpur: a Guru under threat who, tradition says, still kept a court of writers, and Bhai Nand Lal's Persian poems, still sung. Your line was a court of poets.

A family keeps a list on the fridge. Shoes off at the door. Nobody eats until everyone sits. Say thank you to whoever cooked. Nobody voted on it, exactly. It grew out of how the family wanted to live, and somebody finally wrote it down. After the Tenth Guru, Sikhs wrote down lists like that, on a much larger scale: what to do at dawn, how to treat a guest, what to give, what to avoid.
screen: `A LIST ON THE FRIDGE.` → `HOW WE WANT TO LIVE, WRITTEN DOWN.` → `CODES OF HOW A SIKH SHOULD LIVE.`

segments.voice: The word is rehatnama. Rehat is a way of living, a discipline kept day after day. Nama is a written piece, a letter or a record. Together: a written code for living. Tradition links these codes to the circle around Guru Gobind Singh. Some carry the names of Sikhs remembered as close to him; one is linked with Bhai Nand Lal, remembered as a poet of the Guru's court. They were written down after the Guru's time, and that matters for how they're read. They are not scripture. They sit beside the Guru Granth Sahib, not inside it. What do they hold? Mostly ordinary things, which is the point. Rise early. Remember the Name. Bathe and recite the morning prayers. Share what you earn. Keep the hair uncut. Treat the Guru's word with honor. For the Sikhs who wrote them, faith was not only an inner feeling. It was a shape for the whole day. Here's the honest part. The rehatnamas don't all say the same thing. They differ in detail, and some hold lines that later Sikhs questioned or set aside. Scholars and Sikh bodies have read them side by side, and out of that long conversation came a shared code you'll meet later on the path, the Sikh Rehat Maryada. So a rehatnama is a window, not a final word: early Sikhs putting the Gurus' teaching into daily life, written down by people who cared enough to try.
screen: `REHAT, A WAY OF LIVING. NAMA, A WRITING.` · `WRITTEN DOWN AFTER THE GURU'S TIME.` · `A SHAPE FOR THE WHOLE DAY.` · `THEY DIFFER; A SHARED CODE CAME LATER.` · then, large: `A CODE FOR LIVING.`

segments.voice: Think about how you actually want your days to go, not how you think you ought to want them, and find one plain line for your own code, like phone down at the table, or answer kindly before answering fast. Keep it short enough to fit on a fridge, write it down if you have paper, and sit with it to see whether it still fits.
Rehatnama. A written code of Sikh living, linked by tradition to the Tenth Guru's circle and written down after him. Today's word.
Your line: a code for living. Faith with a shape you can see, from dawn on. See you tomorrow.

chat.says: Are the rehatnamas part of the Sikh scripture?
options: No. They're codes written down after the Tenth Guru's time; they sit beside the scripture, not in it.
Yes. They're the closing pages of the Guru Granth Sahib, written by the Tenth Guru himself.
Yes. They're one fixed code that every Sikh body agrees on, word for word.
chat.meaning: The rehatnamas were written down after the Guru's time. They aren't scripture; they sit beside the Guru Granth Sahib, and they differ in detail.
